content: A donor offspring, also referred to as a donor-conceived person, is an individual conceived through the donation of sperm (sperm donation), ova (egg donation), or both. These gametes may come from two separate donors or from a couple. In cases of embryo donation, the conceiving parents are typically a couple. A donor-conceived individual may never discover the true origins of their conception, as information about their biological parent(s) is often not recorded on their birth certificate. This lack of transparency is further exacerbated by the fact that only a small percentage (approximately 10%) of donor-conceived individuals are informed about the nature of their conception by their recipient parent(s). Donor-conceived individuals may have numerous half-siblings as a result of repeated donations from the same donor. In recent years, the voices of donor-conceived individuals have begun to gain recognition globally. Many of those born from anonymous donations express a strong desire to obtain more information about their biological parent(s) in order to complete their personal history. The majority of donor-conceived individuals who are aware of their conception origins oppose the practice of anonymous donation in any form. They argue that such anonymity deprives them of essential knowledge about their genetic background and identity. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, Article 8, emphasizes the importance of preserving a child’s identity. It states: 1. States Parties shall respect the right of the child to preserve their identity, including nationality, name, and family relations as recognized by law, without unlawful interference. 2. If a child is illegally deprived of some or all elements of their identity, States Parties shall provide appropriate assistance and protection with the aim of re-establishing their identity promptly. Donor-conceived individuals should be granted the same rights as others to access information about their genetic history, ensuring their ability to fully understand and preserve their identity.
